title: Soft starter
summary: Ramp a motor up smoothly with a current limit, wire the run signal, and understand why a soft starter is never an isolator.

why.text:
Mixer **MX-1** at the fictional Riverside plant has an 11 kW motor and a belt drive. Started DOL, the belts squeal and slip, and the supply dips. Star-delta would still give a current surge at changeover.

A [[soft starter]] raises the motor voltage gradually, so the current stays under a set limit and the belts take up smoothly.

cards.title: How a soft starter works
cards.text:
Inside are pairs of [[thyristor]]s in each phase. They switch on part-way through each half-cycle of the mains, so the motor sees a reduced voltage. Over the **ramp time** the starter switches them on earlier and earlier until the motor gets full voltage.

Most soft starters then close an internal **bypass** contactor so the thyristors do not run hot.

cards.title: Current limit and torque
cards.text:
Two main settings:
- **Current limit**, as a multiple of FLC (for example 3 × FLC). The starter holds the current at or below this.
- **Ramp time** (for example 8 s).

Torque falls with the **square** of voltage: half voltage gives a quarter of the torque. Set the limit too low and a heavy load will not accelerate.

cards.title: The circuit
cards.text:
Here: **Q1** MPCB → **KM1** line contactor → **SS1** soft starter → **F2** overload → **M1**.

The soft starter gets its **run signal** at IN1-COM from KM1 auxiliary 43-44. So START pulls in KM1, which connects the supply and then tells the soft starter to ramp up. STOP drops KM1 and removes both.

cards.title: Phase loss protection
cards.text:
A soft starter checks its supply. If a phase is missing when it is told to run, it trips with a **FAULT** and will not start. Find the cause (a blown fuse, an open contactor pole, a loose wire), then reset it.

This protects the motor from single-phasing.

cards.title: Not an isolator
cards.text:
Thyristors are semiconductors. When the soft starter is stopped they are "off", but they are **not** an isolating gap, and a failed thyristor can pass full voltage.

The motor terminals can be live with the soft starter stopped. Before work on the motor or cable: isolate at **Q1**, lock off and **prove dead**. Also disconnect the soft starter before an insulation test of the motor circuit.

cards.title: Soft starter or drive?
cards.text:
A soft starter only controls **starting** (and often stopping). Once up to speed the motor runs at full speed on the mains.

If the process needs **variable speed**, you need a variable frequency drive (VFD), which is Module 4.

show.intro: This soft starter is wired correctly. Watch the motor current stay under the limit during the ramp.

tasks.text: Press **START (S1)**. KM1 pulls in and the soft starter starts ramping. The current stays at or below 3 × FLC (about 62 A).
Measure the run signal **SS1 IN1 to COM** in V=. It reads 24 V through KM1 43-44.
Wait for the ramp to finish. The motor reaches full speed and the current falls to FLC.
Press **STOP (S0)**. KM1 drops out and the motor coasts to a stop.

checks.fail: A protective device tripped as soon as power was applied.
The 24 V supply G1 is off.
KM1 pulls in without anyone pressing START.
The motor runs before START is pressed.
START does not pull in and hold KM1. Trace G1 + through S0, F2 95-96, S1 (with KM1 13-14 in parallel) to KM1 A1, then A2 to 0 V.
One second after START the motor is not ramping up. The soft starter needs all three phases from KM1 and a 24 V run signal on IN1-COM (through KM1 43-44).
Starting current is above the soft starter's limit of 3 × FLC. The motor may be bypassing the soft starter.
The motor did not reach full speed at the end of the ramp. Check all three output phases 2T1, 4T2, 6T3 through F2 to the motor.
STOP does not drop out KM1.
After STOP the motor still has power.

guided.intro: The power circuit and the 24 V supply are wired. **Wire the control circuit**: holding contact, KM1 coil, and the soft starter run signal.
hints: Holding contact in parallel with START: S1:13 to KM1:13, S1:14 to KM1:14.
S1:14 feeds the KM1 coil (A1); KM1:A2 returns to G1 −.
Run signal: G1 + to KM1:43, KM1:44 to SS1:IN1, and SS1:COM back to G1 −.

unguided.intro: Now wire the **soft starter power connections** (in from KM1, out to F2) and the **control circuit**, with no hints.

break.intro: This soft starter circuit has **one hidden fault**. Start it, read the soft starter display and the event log, then find the cause by measuring. In this simulator you may measure voltage with the power on. On a real panel, live testing is only allowed when it is justified, by a competent person, following the site risk assessment and GS38. Switch off Q1 before any Ω test.

faults.report: KM1 pole 5-6 is open: the soft starter sees a phase missing and trips.
KM1 auxiliary contact 43-44 does not close: the soft starter never gets its run signal.
The wire from SS1 COM to G1 0 V is broken.
Overload contact F2 95-96 is open, although the overload has not tripped.
The wire from SS1 4T2 to F2 terminal 3 is broken: the motor gets two phases.

extraReports: Nothing is wrong with the circuit.

questions.text: How does a soft starter reduce the starting current?
options: It lowers the motor voltage during the start, then ramps it up
It connects the motor in star
It adds resistance in the earth wire
questions.explain: Thyristors switch on part-way through each half-cycle, giving a reduced voltage that rises over the ramp time.

questions.text: The soft starter halves the motor voltage. What happens to the motor torque?
options: It falls to about a quarter
questions.explain: Torque is roughly proportional to voltage squared.

questions.text: The soft starter is stopped (no run signal). Is it safe to work on the motor terminals?
options: No. Isolate at Q1, lock off and prove dead: thyristors are not an isolator
Yes, if the display says OFF
questions.explain: A stopped or failed soft starter can still have voltage on its output. Only a locked-off isolator and a dead test make it safe.

questions.text: The soft starter shows a phase-loss FAULT. What do you do?
options: Find and fix the missing phase (fuse, contactor pole, loose wire), then reset
Keep pressing START until it runs
questions.explain: The trip protects the motor from single-phasing. Resetting without finding the cause will just trip again.

questions.text: The process needs the mixer to run at different speeds. Is a soft starter suitable?
options: No, it only controls starting and stopping; use a VFD
Yes, if a bypass is fitted
questions.explain: After the ramp, a soft-started motor runs at full mains speed.

questions.text: Before an insulation resistance test on the motor cable, what do you do about the soft starter?
options: Isolate, prove dead and disconnect the soft starter, following the maker's instructions
questions.explain: The test voltage can damage the electronics, and the circuit must be dead first.

questions.text: The current limit is set too low for a heavily loaded mixer. What happens?
options: The motor does not have enough torque to accelerate and may stall or trip
questions.explain: Lower current means lower torque. The load may never reach speed.

apply.intro: Do this on the training bench while your trainer watches. Your trainer signs it off. An app score alone never makes anyone competent or authorised.

items.text: Carries out safe isolation, including the soft starter output side, before starting work.
Wires the line contactor, soft starter, overload and run signal to the drawing and the maker's connection diagram.
Sets current limit and ramp time from the job sheet and records the settings.
Carries out insulation resistance tests with the soft starter disconnected, and records them.
Functional test with the trainer: smooth ramp, current within the limit (clamp meter), STOP, overload trip, phase loss trip and reset.
